nameStory: The name 'sharp-glumed manna-grass' comes from the pointed tips of its glumes - the small bracts that protect each grass flower. The 'manna' part refers to the sweet, edible seeds that many grasses in this genus produce, reminiscent of the biblical manna that sustained wanderers in the wilderness.
description: Sharp-glumed manna-grass is a perennial wetland grass that forms creeping colonies through underground stems called rhizomes. It typically grows 2-4 feet tall with narrow, flat leaves and delicate, open flower clusters that appear in mid to late summer. This grass has a somewhat sprawling growth habit, often leaning or bending rather than standing perfectly upright, and it's found primarily in wet meadows and marsh edges throughout the northeastern United States.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Delicate, open flower clusters (called panicles) with small, purplish-green spikelets that have distinctly sharp-pointed glumes - run your finger gently along them to feel the pointed tips

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeping perennial that spreads by underground rhizomes, often forming loose colonies with stems that lean or bend rather than standing rigidly upright

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat leaf blades that are typically 4-8 inches long with a smooth texture and prominent parallel veins typical of grasses

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, brownish seeds that are mildly sweet to taste when mature - historically eaten by both wildlife and humans

habitat: Sharp-glumed manna-grass thrives in wet meadows, marsh edges, stream banks, and other consistently moist to wet soils. It prefers areas with full to partial sun and can tolerate seasonal flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside other wetland grasses and sedges in low-lying areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from creeping rhizomes, with fresh green leaves unfurling. The plant begins its active growing season as soil temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in mid to late summer, producing the characteristic open, delicate flower clusters with sharp-pointed glumes. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse, while leaves may begin to yellow. The above-ground portions start to die back as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, but the underground rhizome system remains alive and ready to sprout new growth in spring.

funFact: This grass is so rare in New England that it has been documented only once in the entire region - making any sighting a truly remarkable botanical discovery that would excite grass specialists across the continent!
confusionNotes: Sharp-glumed manna-grass can be confused with other wetland grasses, but the key is in the name - gently feel the flower parts (glumes) for those distinctly sharp, pointed tips. Most other grasses in wet areas have blunt or rounded glume tips.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'creeping mannagrass' in some references, this species is extremely rare in New England and represents the far eastern edge of its natural range. Don't expect to find it on casual nature walks - this is a true botanical treasure.
compareHints: Among its manna-grass relatives, sharp-glumed manna-grass is distinguished by those pointed glumes that give it its name. Most other Glyceria species like fowl mannagrass or floating mannagrass have blunt, rounded glume tips. The creeping growth habit also sets it apart from the more upright American manna grass, which grows much taller and more robust.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the mannagrasses, rattlesnake mannagrass is the only one with the distinctive mottled leaf sheaths that give it its name.

Among New England's mannagrasses, blunt mannagrass is distinguished by its rounded flower parts - rattlesnake mannagrass has distinctly sharp-pointed scales, while fowl mannagrass is much smaller overall.
Among New England's mannagrasses, fowl mannagrass is distinguished by its smaller size and fewer florets per spikelet (under 6) compared to larger species like American manna grass.

Among its mannagrass relatives, Slender Mannagrass is distinguished by its delicate build and preference for smaller wetland areas, while American Manna Grass grows much larger and Fowl Mannagrass has more compact flower clusters.
Among the manna grasses, boreal manna grass stands out for its exceptional flexibility and preference for floating or lying flat on water surfaces.
American mannagrass is the giant of its family, much larger and more robust than relatives like fowl mannagrass or floating mannagrass.
**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM - limited reference material]** Unlike its relatives fowl mannagrass and American mannagrass which grow firmly rooted in wet soil, floating mannagrass creates buoyant mats.
**[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Unlike its more common relatives like fowl mannagrass or American mannagrass, limp mannagrass has the distinctive drooping growth habit that gives it its name.
